financial-accounting.overview: Financial Accounting & Reporting under IFRS (Weygandt/Kimmel). Built from your resume (Ch 1–11), the Ch 14 cash-flow summary and the Ch 15 slides. Exam formula sheet: FHNW_FAR Formulae.pdf (provided in the exam).

summary.heading: Ch 1 · Accounting in action
points: Accounting = identify, record and communicate economic events.
IFRS is the international (European) standard; US GAAP is the US standard.
Historical cost principle: record assets at cost. Fair value principle: report some assets at fair value.
Qualities of useful information: relevance (can change a decision) and faithful representation.
Monetary unit assumption: only record what can be expressed in money. Economic entity assumption: keep the business separate from its owners.

terms.def: resources the business owns/controls (cash, receivables, inventory, equipment…)
claims against assets: debts and obligations (accounts payable, loans…)
owners' claim: share capital + retained earnings (revenues − expenses − dividends)

summary.heading: Ch 2 · The recording process
points: An account has a title, a left (debit) side and a right (credit) side.
Steps: analyse the transaction → journalize → post to the ledger.
Show the balance on the side that has more.
Trial balance: list of all accounts and balances at a date; total debits must equal total credits.
Supplies = items bought to consume; unearned service revenue = cash received before the service is performed (a liability).

summary.heading: Ch 3 · Adjusting the accounts
points: Time period assumption: divide the business life into periods (months, quarters, fiscal year).
Accrual basis (IFRS): record revenue when the service is performed and expenses when incurred. Cash basis is not IFRS.
Every adjusting entry has one income statement account and one statement of financial position account — never Cash.
Deferrals (cash first): prepaid expenses, unearned revenues. Accruals (service first): accrued revenues, accrued expenses.
Depreciation is cost allocation, not valuation; shown with contra account Accumulated Depreciation. Book value = cost − accumulated depreciation.
The adjusted trial balance is the basis for the financial statements.

summary.heading: Ch 4 · Completing the cycle & classified balance sheet
points: Temporary accounts (revenues, expenses, dividends) are closed to retained earnings; permanent accounts are never closed.
Post-closing trial balance contains only permanent accounts.
Correcting entries are needed only when errors are found, and are posted before closing.
Classified statement of financial position: intangible assets (incl. goodwill), PP&E less accumulated depreciation, long-term investments, current assets; equity; non-current and current liabilities.
Current = expected to be converted to cash / settled within one year or the operating cycle.

summary.heading: Ch 5 · Merchandising operations
points: Perpetual system: cost of goods sold recorded at each sale. Periodic system: COGS determined by a count at period end.
Purchases are debited to Inventory (perpetual).
FOB shipping point: buyer pays freight; FOB destination: seller pays (Freight-out = seller's operating expense).
Purchase returns/allowances and purchase discounts reduce Inventory.
Sales Returns & Allowances and Sales Discounts are contra-revenue accounts (debit balance).
Other income/expense: items outside the core business (interest, dividends, rent revenue, gains/losses on disposal).
formulas: Beginning inventory + Purchases = Goods available for sale
Goods available for sale − Ending inventory = COGS
Gross profit rate = Gross profit / Net sales

summary.heading: Ch 6 · Inventories
points: Physical count checks records and finds losses (perpetual) or determines inventory and COGS (periodic).
Goods in transit belong to whoever holds legal title (terms of sale). Consigned goods are not owned by the consignee.
Specific identification is rare (art, instruments). Cost flow assumptions: FIFO (earliest costs go to COGS first) and average-cost (weighted-average unit cost).
Lower of cost and net realisable value (LCNRV): report the lower amount.
High inventory = high carrying costs; low inventory = stock-outs.

summary.heading: Ch 8 · Receivables
points: Types: accounts receivable, notes receivable, other receivables.
Report receivables at cash (net) realisable value.
Direct write-off method: Dr Bad Debt Expense, Cr Accounts Receivable — not acceptable under IFRS.
Allowance method (required): estimate at period end — Dr Bad Debt Expense, Cr Allowance for Doubtful Accounts.
Write-off under the allowance method: Dr Allowance, Cr Accounts Receivable — cash realisable value does not change.
Percentage-of-receivables: required allowance balance − existing balance = bad debt expense.
Selling receivables: to a factor (fee 1–3%) or via credit cards (fee 2–4%, recorded like cash sales).
formulas: Cash realisable value = Accounts receivable − Allowance for doubtful accounts

summary.heading: Ch 9 · Plant assets & intangibles
points: Record at cost: all expenditures to acquire the asset and make it ready for use (land: price, closing costs, commissions; equipment: price, taxes, freight, transit insurance, installation and testing). Insurance and licences during use are expenses.
Land is not depreciated; land improvements, buildings and equipment are.
Ordinary repairs = revenue expenditures (expense). Additions/improvements = capital expenditures (debit the asset).
Disposals: retirement, sale (gain if price > book value, loss if lower), exchange. Update depreciation to the disposal date first.
Intangibles (patents, copyrights, franchises, trademarks, goodwill): limited life → amortise; indefinite life → no amortisation.
formulas: Units-of-activity = (Cost − Residual value) / Total units × Units used

summary.heading: Ch 10–11 · Liabilities
points: Current liability: paid within one year or the operating cycle (notes payable, accounts payable, unearned revenue, accrued liabilities, VAT/sales tax payable, current maturities of long-term debt).
VAT is collected at each stage of the supply chain; sales tax only once at final sale.
Provision: recognise only if (1) present obligation from a past event, (2) outflow probable (more likely than not), (3) reliable estimate. Example: product warranties, expensed in the period of sale.
Liquidity = ability to pay maturing obligations.
formulas: Current ratio = Current assets / Current liabilities (above 1 is good)

summary.heading: Ch 14 · Statement of cash flows
points: Operating activities ↔ current assets and current liabilities; investing ↔ investments and non-current assets; financing ↔ non-current liabilities and equity.
Indirect method: start with net income, add depreciation/amortisation, add losses and deduct gains, then adjust for changes in non-cash current assets and current liabilities.
Increase in a current asset → subtract; decrease → add. Increase in a current liability → add; decrease → subtract.
Direct method: cash revenues minus cash expenses.

summary.heading: Ch 15 · Financial analysis
points: Horizontal (trend) analysis: change over time vs a base year, in amount or %.
Vertical (common-size) analysis: each item as % of a base (total assets or net sales); lets you compare companies of different sizes.
Ratio groups: liquidity, profitability, solvency.
formulas: Change % = (Current year − Base year) / Base year
Acid-test = (Cash + Short-term investments + Receivables) / Current liabilities
AR turnover = Net credit sales / Average net AR

cards.a: Assets = Liabilities + Equity
IFRS: international standard (used in Europe). GAAP: US standard.
Record assets at their cost (what was paid when acquired).
Only transactions that can be expressed in money are recorded.
The business's activities are kept separate from its owners and other entities.

cards.q: Which accounts increase with a debit?
cards.a: Assets, expenses and dividends.

cards.q: Which accounts increase with a credit?
cards.a: Liabilities, equity (share capital, retained earnings) and revenues.
A list of all accounts and their balances at a given time; total debits must equal total credits.
Liability: cash received before the service is performed.
Accrual: revenue when performed, expenses when incurred (IFRS). Cash: when cash moves (not IFRS).

cards.q: Name the four types of adjusting entries.
cards.a: Deferrals: prepaid expenses, unearned revenues. Accruals: accrued revenues, accrued expenses.

cards.q: Two rules for every adjusting entry
cards.a: It never involves Cash, and it affects one income statement account and one balance sheet account.

cards.q: Supplies €2,500 bought, €1,000 on hand at month end. Adjusting entry?
cards.a: Dr Supplies Expense €1,500 / Cr Supplies €1,500.

cards.q: Note payable €5,000 at 12%, one month of accrued interest?
cards.a: 5,000 × 12% × 1/12 = €50. Dr Interest Expense 50 / Cr Interest Payable 50.
No. It allocates an asset's cost to the periods it is used.
Cost − Accumulated depreciation.
Temporary (revenues, expenses, dividends) are closed to retained earnings each period; permanent (balance sheet) accounts are never closed.

cards.q: What does the post-closing trial balance contain?
cards.a: Only permanent (statement of financial position) accounts.
An intangible asset: the established reputation of a business, recognised when a business is acquired.
Perpetual: COGS recorded at each sale with detailed records. Periodic: COGS determined at period end by a count.
Beginning inventory + Purchases = Goods available for sale; − Ending inventory = COGS.

cards.q: FOB shipping point — who pays freight?
cards.a: The buyer (ownership passes when goods leave the seller).

cards.q: Sales returns & allowances is what kind of account?
cards.a: A contra-revenue account with a debit balance.
Gross profit / Net sales.
First-in, first-out: the earliest costs go to COGS first; ending inventory uses the most recent costs.

cards.q: Inventory turnover and days in inventory
cards.a: Turnover = COGS / Average inventory. Days = 365 / Turnover.

cards.q: Who includes consigned goods in inventory?
cards.a: The consignor (owner), not the consignee who sells them.
Lower of cost and net realisable value: report inventory at the lower amount.

cards.q: Why is the direct write-off method not allowed under IFRS?
cards.a: It doesn't match bad debt expense with revenue and doesn't show receivables at cash realisable value.

cards.q: Allowance method: entry to record estimated bad debts
cards.a: Dr Bad Debt Expense / Cr Allowance for Doubtful Accounts.

cards.q: Allowance method: entry to write off a specific account
cards.a: Dr Allowance for Doubtful Accounts / Cr Accounts Receivable. Cash realisable value stays the same.
A finance company or bank that buys receivables and collects them, charging 1–3%.

cards.q: Which plant asset is not depreciated, and why?
cards.a: Land: its usefulness and revenue-producing ability stay intact.
Repairs: revenue expenditure (expense). Additions/improvements: capital expenditure (debit the asset).
(Cost − Residual value) / Useful life
2 × straight-line rate, applied to book value each year.

cards.q: Sale of a plant asset: when is there a gain?
cards.a: When the sale price is higher than the book value.
Not amortised (tested for impairment instead).

cards.q: Three conditions to recognise a provision
cards.a: Present obligation from a past event; probable outflow; reliable estimate.
VAT is collected at every stage of the supply chain; sales tax only once at the final sale.
Current assets / Current liabilities; above 1 means current assets cover current liabilities.

cards.q: Three sections of the statement of cash flows
cards.a: Operating, investing, financing activities.

cards.q: Indirect method: steps from net income
cards.a: Net income + depreciation/amortisation + losses − gains ± changes in non-cash current assets and current liabilities.

cards.q: Accounts receivable increased. Effect on operating cash flow (indirect)?
cards.a: Subtract the increase.

cards.q: Accounts payable increased. Effect on operating cash flow (indirect)?
cards.a: Add the increase.
Horizontal: change over time vs a base year. Vertical: each item as % of a base amount in the same year.
(Cash + Short-term investments + Receivables) / Current liabilities — immediate liquidity.
365 / Accounts receivable turnover.

questions.q: Which principle requires recording assets at their purchase price?
questions.explain: Historical cost: assets are recorded at what they cost.

questions.q: Which account normally has a credit balance?
questions.explain: Unearned service revenue is a liability, so it increases with credits.

questions.q: A company receives €1,200 in advance for 3 months of service. After one month, the adjusting entry is…
options: Dr Unearned Service Revenue 400 / Cr Service Revenue 400
Dr Service Revenue 400 / Cr Unearned Service Revenue 400
questions.explain: One-third of the service is performed, so move €400 from the liability to revenue.

questions.q: Employees earn €400/day; 3 days are unpaid at month end. The adjustment is…
options: Dr Salaries Expense 1,200 / Cr Salaries Payable 1,200
questions.explain: Accrued expense: increase the expense and the liability. Adjusting entries never touch Cash.

questions.q: Equipment cost €5,000 and depreciation is €40 per month. Book value after one month?
questions.explain: Book value = cost − accumulated depreciation = 5,000 − 40.

questions.q: Which account is closed at the end of the period?
questions.explain: Revenues are temporary accounts and are closed to retained earnings.

questions.q: Beginning inventory €10,000, purchases €40,000, ending inventory €15,000. COGS?
Under FOB destination, freight costs are paid by…
questions.explain: The seller is responsible until the goods reach the destination.

questions.q: Under FIFO, ending inventory is valued at…
questions.explain: The earliest costs go to COGS, so the latest costs stay in inventory.

questions.q: COGS €1,281,000 and average inventory €560,000. Inventory turnover is about…
questions.explain: 1,281,000 / 560,000 ≈ 2.3 times (≈159 days in inventory).

questions.q: Under the allowance method, writing off a specific uncollectible account…
questions.explain: Both AR and the allowance fall by the same amount.

questions.q: Which method for bad debts is required under IFRS?
questions.explain: The allowance method matches expenses with revenues.

questions.q: Equipment €12,000, residual €2,000, life 5 years. Straight-line depreciation per year?
Which cost is NOT capitalised as part of equipment?
options: Annual insurance after it's in use
questions.explain: Recurring insurance during use is an expense.

questions.q: Equipment with book value €3,000 is sold for €2,200. Result?
questions.explain: Sale price below book value → loss on disposal.

questions.q: Which is NOT a condition for recognising a provision?
options: Present obligation from a past event
questions.explain: A provision is recognised before any payment.

questions.q: Current assets €300,000, current liabilities €150,000. Current ratio?
Buying equipment for cash is classified as…
questions.explain: Non-current assets belong to investing activities.

questions.q: Indirect method: net income €50,000, depreciation €8,000, increase in AR €5,000. Operating cash flow?
Issuing shares for cash is a…
questions.explain: Equity and non-current liabilities are financing.

questions.q: Expressing each expense as a % of net sales is…
questions.explain: Vertical (common-size) analysis uses a base amount from the same year.

questions.q: AR turnover is 10.2. Average collection period is about…

organisational-behaviour.overview: Organisational Behaviour with Prof. Dr. Anita Graf (Mon 13:15–15:00, Olten). Built from your resume. Exam: Moopad, K-Prim and A+/− questions, 75 minutes, 60 points, no aids. Admission: 8 of 10 Moodle assignments submitted on time.

summary.heading: Learning
points: Learning is a key competence for studies and work: developing the ability to act, lifelong.
Long-term memory needs attention and active processing. Learning physically changes the brain (plasticity); new knowledge links to prior knowledge and needs time and repetition.
'Learning types' are a myth: preference ≠ effectiveness. Use all senses and learn actively.
Motivational-volitional factors: motivation, attribution style ('it's due to how hard I try'), self-concept, self-control and self-regulation.

summary.heading: Learning strategies & techniques
points: Multi-store memory model: sensory → working memory → long-term memory.
Wild (2005): memorisation/repetition (surface), organisation/structuring (depth), elaboration (depth: link new to known).
Metacognitive strategies: planning, monitoring, regulating.
Techniques: mind maps, concept maps, PQ4R (Preview, Questions, Read, Reflect, Recite, Review), Cornell notes, loci technique, spaced repetition (Leitner box), practice testing (very powerful).

summary.heading: Self-management
points: Self-management competence: willingness and capacity to take ownership of your life to sustain performance capability, willingness to perform, well-being and balance.

Dynamic core model: self-responsibility, self-awareness, self-development, goals, time & information, physical & mental health, social relationships, self-control & self-regulation, other aspects (self-efficacy, resilience).
Three E's of time management: Effectiveness (right things), Efficiency (things right), Energy (use daily energy well).

Methods: ALPEN, Eisenhower matrix, MoSCoW, Rule of Three, time blocking, deep work, 2-minute rule, eat the frog, Pomodoro. Micro-breaks (30 s–10 min) help concentration, performance, health, stress and motivation.

terms.def: Activities, Length, Padding (plan max 60%), Establish priorities, Note/check
important+urgent: do now; important+not urgent: schedule; urgent+not important: delegate; neither: drop

summary.heading: Stress
points: Distress = negative (burden); eustress = positive (manageable challenge). Balance activation and regeneration.
Stress triad: stressors (demanding conditions) → personal stress amplifiers (inner drivers: be strong, be perfect, be popular) → stress response.
Stress response on three levels: physical (heart rate, breathing), behavioural (skipping breaks, restlessness), cognitive-emotional (helplessness, anxiety, carousel of thoughts).

summary.heading: Groups & teams
points: Formal group: defined by the organisation. Informal group: voluntary, social. Working group: mainly exchange information. Working team: coordinated collaboration toward a shared goal.
Optimal size about 4–6. Larger groups risk social loafing / free-riding → define each person's contribution.
Roles: role expectations, perceptions, multiple roles. Belbin: Plant (ideas), Coordinator (decisions), Shaper (implementation).
Five requirements for effective teamwork: clear communication, defined roles, mutual respect, effective problem-solving, clear focus on objectives (and celebrate success).

summary.heading: Conflict
points: Conflict: experienced incompatibility between beliefs or interests of at least two parties, plus their actions to overcome it. A disruption is temporary and easily resolved.
Causes: relationship, evaluation (goal importance), assessment (how to reach the same goal), distribution (scarce resource).
Forms: latent vs open, hot vs cold, strong vs weak.
Relationship and task conflicts both correlate negatively with satisfaction and performance (relationship conflicts more strongly).
If the manager is part of the conflict and escalation is advanced → independent expert. If not → mediator. Regulation via power, rights ('who is right?'), interests (negotiation), or self-regulation.

summary.heading: Personality
points: Personality: the sum of an individual's ways of reacting and interacting; described through relatively stable, measurable traits.
Determinants: disposition vs environment (twin studies).
Tests are used in selection, job fit and career planning. Self-assessments suffer from impression management; observer judgements predict job success better.
Big Five (OCEAN) is the main model. Dark triad: narcissism, Machiavellianism, psychopathy — negative traits that can still correlate with career success.

summary.heading: Reflection
points: Reflection: ability to challenge yourself, others and systems to enable constructive development.
Success factors: time and space, accept discomfort, methods and guiding questions, regular routine, other perspectives, document and act.
Four dimensions: level (individual, team, system), content, depth (analytical, evaluative, transformative), method.
Methods: start-stop-continue, 5W, journaling, Gibbs cycle (description, feelings, evaluation, analysis, conclusion, action plan).

summary.heading: Emotions
points: Affect = umbrella term. Emotion = short and intense (seconds/minutes). Mood = longer (hours/days), no clear cause. Feeling = specific subjective experience.
Components: cognitive (appraisal), physiological, motivational (readiness to act), expressive, subjective.
Circumplex model classifies emotions. Affective events theory (Weiss & Cropanzano, 1996): work events → affective reactions → attitudes and behaviour (judgement-driven vs affect-driven).
Emotion regulation motives: hedonic, instrumental, prosocial. Needs discrepancy perception.
Strategies: situation selection, situation modification, attentional deployment, cognitive reappraisal; or regulate the response (arousal, feeling, expression).
Emotional labour: deliberately inducing or suppressing feelings at work to create an intended effect on others.

summary.heading: Motivation
points: Motivation: processes that determine intensity, direction and persistence of effort toward a goal.
McClelland: needs for achievement, power, affiliation.
Equity theory (Adams): compare your inputs/outcomes with others; distributive and procedural justice.
Goal-setting theory (Locke & Latham): specific, challenging goals + feedback raise performance.
Vroom VIE: motivation = expectancy × instrumentality × valence.

Self-determination theory: intrinsic vs extrinsic motivation; three basic needs (autonomy, competence, relatedness). Rewards, punishment, controlling feedback, deadlines and competition can undermine intrinsic motivation.
Regulation qualities: external → introjected → identified → intrinsic.

summary.heading: Perception
points: Perception: organising and interpreting sensory impressions; behaviour is based on perceived reality.
Process: stimuli → sensory input → neural processing → perception → recognition. Bottom-up (data-driven) vs top-down (knowledge-driven).
Biases: halo/horns, contrast effect, similar-to-me, stereotypes.
Johari window: open, blind, hidden, unknown — reduce blind spots via feedback.
Attribution (Kelley covariation): consensus, distinctiveness, consistency. Errors: fundamental attribution error, self-serving bias.

summary.heading: Decision-making
points: Models: rational (homo economicus), bounded rationality (satisficing), intuition.
Group decisions: more ideas, acceptance, learning vs more time, conflict, groupthink.
Biases: overconfidence, confirmation, anchoring, availability, escalation of commitment, loss aversion and framing, hindsight, outcome bias.
Better decisions: define objectives, question assumptions, evaluate more options.
AI: fast analysis and pattern recognition, but risks of over-trust, inherited bias and wrong outputs.

cards.q: Two conditions for storing information in long-term memory
cards.a: Attention and active processing.
No — it's a myth. Learning preference is not learning effectiveness; use all senses actively.
Memorisation/repetition (surface), organisation/structuring and elaboration (both depth-oriented).
Planning, monitoring, regulating.
Preview, Questions, Read, Reflect, Recite, Review.
Reviewing at increasing intervals (Ebbinghaus forgetting curve), e.g. Leitner box system.

cards.q: Which technique is 'very powerful' for retention?
cards.a: Practice testing (retrieval practice).
Effectiveness (right things), Efficiency (things right), Energy (use daily energy well).
Activities, Length, Padding (plan max 60%), Establish priorities, Note-taking/checking.

cards.q: Eisenhower matrix: important but not urgent
cards.a: Schedule and plan it.
Fixed work intervals with short breaks; a longer break after 3–4 intervals.
Distress: perceived as a burden. Eustress: a manageable challenge that can motivate.
Stressors, personal stress amplifiers, stress response.

cards.q: Three levels of the stress response
cards.a: Physical, observable behaviour, cognitive-emotional.
Group: mainly exchanges information. Team: coordinated collaboration toward a common goal.

cards.q: Optimal group size and main risk of large groups
cards.a: About 4–6; risk of social loafing/free-riding.
Plant (creative ideas), Coordinator (decisions), Shaper (implementation).
Clear communication, defined roles, mutual respect, effective problem-solving, clear focus on objectives.
Relationship, evaluation, assessment, distribution.
Parties want the same goal but disagree on how to achieve it.
Hot: open fierce arguing. Cold: no outward dispute, feelings are repressed.

cards.q: Four ways a mediator can regulate conflict
cards.a: Power, rights ('who is right'), interests (negotiation), self-regulation.
Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, Neuroticism.

cards.q: What predicts job success better than self-assessments?
cards.a: Observer judgements.
Narcissism, Machiavellianism, psychopathy.
Description, Feelings, Evaluation, Analysis, Conclusion, Action plan.
Analytical, evaluative, transformative.
Emotion: short, intense, has a cause. Mood: longer (hours/days), cause unclear.
Cognitive (appraisal), physiological, motivational, expressive, subjective.
Changing how you think about a situation to change the emotion.
Inducing or suppressing feelings at work to create a desired effect on others.
Intensity, direction, persistence.
Motivation depends on Expectancy (effort→outcome), Instrumentality (outcome→consequence) and Valence (value).
Monetary rewards, punishment, controlling feedback, deadlines, competition.

cards.q: Qualities of motivation (SDT), from least to most self-determined
cards.a: External → introjected → identified regulation → intrinsic motivation.
Specific, challenging goals plus feedback improve performance.
One positive (halo) or negative (horns) trait dominates the overall judgement.
Judging someone relative to people seen just before.
Consensus, distinctiveness, consistency.
Over-weighting internal (personal) causes and under-weighting the situation when judging others.
Success → internal causes; failure → external causes.
Choosing the first 'good enough' option under bounded rationality.
Relying heavily on the first figure given, e.g. in salary negotiations.
Sticking with a failing decision because resources are already invested.
Judging a decision by its result instead of the decision process.

questions.q: Which strategy is surface-level according to Wild (2005)?
questions.explain: Rote repetition doesn't build deep understanding.

questions.q: Which technique is based on the Ebbinghaus forgetting curve?
questions.explain: Spaced repetition reviews at increasing intervals.

questions.q: In the ALPEN method, how much of your day should you plan?
questions.explain: P = padding: keep buffer time.

questions.q: Urgent but not important tasks (Eisenhower) should be…
questions.explain: Delegate, or handle quickly with minimum time.

questions.q: 'Be perfect' and 'be strong' are examples of…
questions.explain: They're beliefs that make you put yourself under stress.

questions.q: Social loafing is most likely when…
options: The group has 4 members with clear tasks
questions.explain: Free-riding grows when contributions are invisible.

questions.q: Two colleagues fight over the only free meeting room. This is a…
questions.explain: A dispute over a scarce resource.

questions.q: A latent conflict…
options: Exists but hasn't led to hostile behaviour yet
questions.explain: Latent conflicts can 'break out' into open conflicts.

questions.q: Self-assessment personality tests are weakened mainly by…
options: Low reliability of the Big Five
questions.explain: People present themselves favourably.

questions.q: In the Gibbs cycle, which step comes right after 'Feelings'?
questions.explain: Description → Feelings → Evaluation → Analysis → Conclusion → Action plan.

questions.q: A short, intense reaction lasting seconds to minutes is a(n)…
questions.explain: Moods last longer and have no clear cause.

questions.q: Thinking 'this criticism helps me improve' to feel less hurt is…
questions.explain: Reappraisal changes the interpretation of the situation.

questions.q: According to SDT, which can undermine intrinsic motivation?
questions.explain: Deadlines threaten feelings of autonomy.

questions.q: In Vroom's model, 'valence' is…
options: Belief that effort leads to performance
The value of the outcome to the person
The link between performance and reward
questions.explain: Valence = how much the outcome is valued.

questions.q: Comparing your pay-to-effort ratio with a colleague's relates to…
questions.explain: Adams' equity theory is about social comparison.

questions.q: An average candidate is rated poorly after a brilliant one. This is the…
questions.explain: Judgements are influenced by who you saw before.

questions.q: 'I passed because I studied; I failed because the exam was unfair.' This is…
questions.explain: Success internal, failure external.

questions.q: Continuing a failing project because a lot was already invested is…
questions.explain: Sunk costs keep people committed.

questions.q: Bounded rationality leads people to…
questions.explain: Limited time, information and capacity → good-enough choices.

critical-thinking.overview: Critical Thinking & Academic Writing (Mon 15:30–19:00). Built from your resume. Research Paper Proposal due on Moodle 13 Dec 2026, 23:59; Critical Thinking exam on Moodle (MooPad mock exam on 30 Nov).

summary.heading: Thinking & critical thinking
points: System 1: fast, automatic (saying hello). System 2: slow, deliberate (buying a house, choosing studies).
Critical thinking is not negative: it is the art of analysing and evaluating thinking with a view to improving it — analyse information and arguments carefully, from different angles.
Obstacles: overthinking, lack of time, relying on AI, information overload, emotions, lack of practice or freedom.

summary.heading: Media & information literacy
points: Assess sources by authorship, format, audience, content and purpose.
Academic sources: peer-reviewed, written for a scholarly audience, full bibliography.
Misinformation: false but shared believing it's true. Disinformation: false and spread deliberately to influence. Malinformation: true information used to harm.
Lateral reading: don't trust the first source; check what other sources say about it.
Media functions: entertain, educate/inform, public forum, watchdog. Public service media: financed and controlled by the public, independent of state and commercial pressure.
Filter bubble: algorithm-created isolation based on past behaviour. Echo chamber: mainly exposed to views that confirm your beliefs.
Investigative journalism uncovers wrongdoing and holds power accountable — the 'conscience' of journalism.
Facts are objective and verifiable; opinions are not. Related terms: alternative facts, post-truth, propaganda, conspiracy theories, fake news.

summary.heading: Scientific quality criteria
points: Critical rationalism: we can never be certain our findings match reality; critique is the principle.

Criteria: objectivity, honesty, verifiability, reliability (same method → same results), validity (measures what it should), comprehensibility, relevance, logical argumentation, originality, transparency.
Evaluate results: authentic evidence? replicated elsewhere? realistic conditions? possible distortion or bias?

summary.heading: Arguments & fallacies
points: An argument = claim + reason(s).
Fallacy: an unsound argument where the next logical step isn't followed.

terms.def: collapses if one element is removed
A will inevitably lead to Z
exaggerate the opponent's view, then attack it
everyone thinks so, so it's true

summary.heading: Research paper structure
points: 1 Introduction: context, research gap, research question, thesis, aim.
2 Literature review: what is known so far.
3 Research approach (method). 4 Findings. 5 Discussion: link findings to previous research. 6 Conclusion.

summary.heading: Sourcing & writing
points: Academic literature: published scholarly writing, usually peer-reviewed. Grey literature: produced outside traditional publishing channels.
DOI = Digital Object Identifier for an article.
Reference managers: Zotero, Mendeley.
Sessions: in-text citations (direct and indirect quotes), avoiding plagiarism, paraphrasing, paragraph structure, academic style, logical connections, cognitive biases (incl. AI training-data bias).

principles-of-management.overview: Principles of Management (Thu 17:30–21:00), textbook chapters 1–7, 10, 14 and 16. Built from your resume. The guest speaker on 10 Dec (Nathanael Hausmann, Läderach) is mandatory and exam-relevant.

summary.heading: Ch 1 · The exceptional manager
points: Efficiency = using resources (people, money, materials) wisely. Effectiveness = achieving results and the organisation's goals.
Four functions (POLC): Planning, Organising, Leading, Controlling.
Levels: top (CEO, 5–10-year view), middle, first-line (supervisor/foreperson). Functional manager = one activity; general manager = several.
Mintzberg roles: interpersonal (figurehead, leader, liaison), informational (monitor, disseminator, spokesperson), decisional (entrepreneur, disturbance handler, resource allocator, negotiator).
Katz skills: conceptual, human, technical.
Challenges: competitive advantage (innovation, efficiency, quality, customer responsiveness), information technology/AI, diversity, globalisation, ethics, the 17 SDGs, happiness and meaningfulness.
Career readiness = knowledge (hard skills), soft skills, attitudes.

summary.heading: Ch 2 · Management theory
points: Classical: scientific management (Taylor's four principles: study the task scientifically, select the right workers, train and give incentives, plan work methods) and administrative management.
Behavioural: early behaviourism, human relations movement, behavioural science.
Quantitative: operations management (supply chain) and evidence-based management.
Systems view: open vs closed systems, synergy, complexity theory; feedback from inside and outside.
Contingency view: the right approach depends on the situation.
Contemporary: learning organisation, high-performance work practices (build KSAs, motivation, decision opportunities), shared value and sustainable development.

summary.heading: Ch 3 · Stakeholders & environment
points: Shareholder value perspective: maximise value for shareholders. Stakeholder perspective: serve employees, suppliers, customers and society too.
Triple bottom line: People, Planet, Profit.
Stakeholder influence: resource provision, decision influence, accountability/oversight, feedback/innovation.
Managers identify stakeholders, assess their influence, balance interests and communicate.
PESTLE for the macro-environment.

summary.heading: Ch 4 · Global management
points: Globalisation: the collapse of time and distance; why and how companies expand internationally; free trade and regional cooperation; understanding cultural differences.

summary.heading: Ch 5 · Planning
points: Planning = setting goals and deciding how to achieve them; it gives direction, encourages new ideas and builds sustainable competitive advantage.
Strategic (top, long-term), tactical (middle, medium-term), operational (first-line, short-term). Means-end chain links goals across levels.
Mission (why we exist), vision (long-term aspiration, 10–15 years), values statement.
SMART goals: Specific, Measurable, Attainable, Results-oriented, Target date.
Management by objectives (MBO): set objectives jointly → action plans → periodic review → evaluate and reward.
Single-use vs standing plans. Pitfalls: top-down planning, rigid plans, not updating.

summary.heading: Ch 6 · Strategic management
points: Porter: strategy = unique and valuable position, clear trade-offs, fit among activities.
Assess current reality: competitive intelligence, SWOT, PESTEL, forecasting (trend and scenario analysis), benchmarking, VRIO.

Corporate-level: growth (concentration — market penetration, market development, product development; vertical integration — backward/forward; diversification — related/unrelated; international expansion), stability, defensive (turnaround, divestiture, liquidation, bankruptcy). BCG matrix for the portfolio.
Entry modes (low → high control and risk): exporting, licensing, franchising, joint venture, wholly owned subsidiary (greenfield or acquisition).
Global strategy (standardised, high integration, e.g. Coca-Cola) vs multidomestic (locally adapted, e.g. Nestlé).

Business-level: Porter's five forces (new entrants, suppliers, buyers, substitutes, rivalry) and four strategies (cost leadership, differentiation, cost focus, focused differentiation). 'Stuck in the middle' = no clear strategy.
Evaluate options with SAF: Suitability, Acceptability, Feasibility. Implementation: people, strategy, operations; watch for roadblocks.

summary.heading: Ch 7 · Decision making
points: Rational model: identify the problem → generate alternatives → evaluate (ethical? feasible? effective?) → implement and evaluate.
Nonrational: bounded rationality, hubris, satisficing, intuition.
Evidence-based decision making; big data's 5 Vs: Volume, Variety, Velocity, Veracity, Value. Descriptive vs predictive analytics; machine learning.
AI types: automate (robotic), anticipate (algorithmic), analyse (biometric), advise (conversational).
Decision styles (tolerance of ambiguity × value orientation): directive, analytical, conceptual, behavioural.
Biases: availability, representativeness, confirmation, sunk cost, anchoring, overconfidence, hindsight, framing, escalation of commitment, categorical thinking.
Group decisions: groupthink risk; brainstorming rules, devil's advocacy, dialectic method; post-mortem review.

summary.heading: Ch 10 · Change & innovation
points: Reactive change (respond to unexpected problems) vs proactive change (anticipate).
Three forms, least to most threatening: adaptive, innovative, radically innovative.
Lewin's model: unfreezing → changing → refreezing.
Organisational development: multiple interventions, management support, goals, culture.
Innovation: product innovation; incremental vs radical; an innovation system of structures, processes and practices.
Resistance to change = emotional/behavioural response to real or imagined threats to routines.

summary.heading: Ch 14 · Power & influence
points: Leading inspires and engages; managing uses resources to reach goals.
Six sources of power: legitimate, reward, coercive, expert, referent, informational.

summary.heading: Ch 16 · Control
points: Controlling = monitoring performance, comparing with goals, correcting.
Why control: adapt to change, find errors, cut costs, detect opportunities, give feedback, decentralise.
Management by exception: only report significant deviations. Control charts set upper and lower limits.
Feedforward (future), concurrent (present), feedback (past) control.
Balanced scorecard: financial, customer, internal business, innovation and learning perspectives. Strategy map visualises the path.
Budgets: incremental, fixed vs variable. Statements: balance sheet, income statement, cash flows. Functional vs dysfunctional turnover.
TQM: continuous improvement, involve everyone, listen to customers, accurate standards. Deming: PDCA cycle. Six Sigma (DMAIC), Lean Six Sigma, ISO 9000 (quality), ISO 14000 (environment).
